Hook: In the year to August 2023, Micron Technology, America's largest maker of memory chips, sold 15.5 billion dollars' worth of them, and lost 5.7 billion dollars on its operations. Three years later, in the year to September 2026, it sold 133.2 billion dollars' worth, and made an operating profit of 99.3 billion. In its last quarter it kept 81 cents of every dollar of sales as operating profit. Same company. Mostly the same factories. The same kind of chip. What changed was the price of memory, and the price changed because in 2023 the world had too many memory chips, and in 2026 it had too few.

The same thing happens at sea. A.P. Moller-Maersk, the Danish container shipping company, made 1.7 billion dollars of operating profit in 2019. In 2022, with the world's ports jammed and every container booked, it made 30.9 billion. A year later, 3.9 billion. Booms like these do not last, because everyone can see them. Every chip maker and every shipowner sees the same high price, and orders more factories and more ships. They take years to build. And when they arrive, they all arrive together.
Industry, Built. Part six: the cycle. Why do industries keep building too much at the top?
Hogs: Chapter three. Sixty years of hogs.

Ezekiel's model makes a sharp prediction, and America kept the records to test it. For decades the price of hogs was set at the stock yards of Chicago, and the National Bureau of Economic Research later gathered the prices, month by month. Here they are, from 1880 to 1940. And here is how many hogs were slaughtered across the country, over the same years. Both lines wander: wars, depressions, and a country growing. But look closely, and both lines are also shaking, with a rhythm of a few years. That shaking is what we are after.

Take away the slow wandering, the wars, the depressions and the growth of the country, by comparing each month with the average of the five years around it, and keep only the swings around it. In orange, the hog price above or below its own trend. In pink, the number of hogs slaughtered. When one is up, the other is usually down: the correlation between them in the same month is -0.61. More hogs, lower price, exactly as the demand line says. And a high price is followed, about 2 and a half years later, by more hogs. Farmers did respond to price, with a delay. But the delay is longer than Ezekiel's model allows. One full swing of the hogs took about 3.6 years, not two. Part of the reason is biology: to raise more pigs, a farmer first keeps young sows back from market to breed them, so a high price cuts the supply of pork before it raises it. Part of it is people: farmers do not all react at once, and they remember last year as well as this one. Ronald Coase, years before his Nobel prize, made the same objection about British pigs in 1935. The cobweb is the right shape. The real wait is just longer than one season.
Lead: Chapter five. Why the wait makes it worse.

Why does the wait matter so much? Run the same market four times, changing only how long a ship takes to build. If a ship takes one year, owners who order too many find out quickly, and the rate barely moves: a swing of 3 percent. Two years: 11 percent. Three years: 81 percent. Four years, and the rate swings by more than its own average: 130 percent. Nothing else changed. The longer the wait, the longer owners keep ordering against a high rate before the first new ship shows them their mistake, and the bigger the wave that lands at the end. In the real world the waits differ: months for a house, about a year for a pig, years for a ship, a chip plant or an oil field. The model says the industries with the longest waits should have the wildest swings, and the rest of this part is a tour of them.

Everyone in these industries knows about the cycle. So why doesn't it get competed away? First, plants come in lumps. A memory fab or a giant container ship is not a small step: one new plant can add a large slice of the world's capacity in a single go. Second, the orders are hidden. Each owner sees today's price, but not the orders its rivals placed last month, until the ships turn up. Third, lenders lend most at the top. A ship earning a record rate, or a factory full of orders, is the easiest thing in the world to borrow against. And fourth, people. A manager who refuses to build in a boom, and turns out to be right, looks no better than the others when the bust comes, and much worse while the boom lasts.
Ships: Shipping keeps the best record of the wave. Every ship in the world is registered, and so is every ship on order. So you can ask: for every ship sailing today, how many more have been ordered and not yet delivered? In 2009, after the boom of the mid 2000s, the answer was 52 percent, according to the United Nations' trade agency. For every two ships at sea, another one was coming. For the ships that carry coal, ore and grain, it was 78 percent. Those ships had been ordered when freight rates were at records, in 2007 and 2008. They were delivered into the slump of 2009, when world trade shrank. By 2014 the ratio was down to nineteen percent; by the start of 2023, 11. The industry had been burned, and ordered less. By early 2025, it was climbing again: 15 percent. And the average hides the hot spots. For the tankers that carry liquefied natural gas, the ships on order equalled 51 percent of the fleet: one new ship for every two already sailing.

Container shipping has just been round the loop. When the pandemic jammed the world's ports, every box was booked and freight rates exploded. Maersk's operating profit went from under two billion dollars to 31 billion in three years. And the shipowners did what the model says: they ordered. In early 2025, ships equal to a quarter of the whole container fleet were on order. In 2024, container ships made up 41 percent of all the new ship tonnage delivered in the world. Profits fell anyway. For a while, attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which sent them the long way round Africa, used up some of the new capacity. Even so, Maersk's operating profit in 2025 was 3.5 billion dollars, below 2023's. Take the detour away, and the wave of new ships is still out there.
Chips: Memory chips may be the purest cycle in modern industry. A memory chip from one maker does the same job as one from another, so they compete almost entirely on price. A new factory costs many billions of dollars and takes years to build and fill with machines. Demand comes in surges, from personal computers, then phones, then data centres. Here are Micron's sales, every quarter since 2009. Four times, sales peaked, and within two years they fell: by a fifth, by more than a third, by more than two fifths, and in 2023 by 57 percent. And then came the boom of 2025 and 2026, driven by the data centres being built for artificial intelligence. In its last quarter Micron sold 54.2 billion dollars of chips, and kept 81 cents of each dollar as operating profit. A year earlier it had sold 11.3 billion.

And Micron did what the capital cycle predicts. The orange bars are what it spent each year on new factories and machines. The grey line is depreciation: roughly what it would need to spend just to replace the plant that is wearing out. In most years the two move together, with spending somewhat above depreciation as the company grows. In fiscal 2026 Micron spent 30.7 billion dollars, 3.2 times its depreciation: the biggest gap since at least 2010. Notice too what happened after the peak of 2018: in fiscal 2019, with sales down by almost a quarter, Micron spent more on plant than in its record year, because the plant ordered at the top was still being paid for at the bottom. The factories ordered in this boom will arrive over the next few years. Whether demand is still there to meet them is the question every cycle asks.
Houses: Houses take months to build, not years, but there are millions of them, built by thousands of builders who cannot see each other's plans. In America, the Census Bureau counts every month how many homes were started, and how many were finished. In the early 2000s, with prices rising and mortgages easy to get, the number of homes started climbed, to a pace of 2.27 million a year in January 2006. Then it collapsed, by 79 percent in three years. But look at the blue line: the homes being finished. They kept coming for a year after the starts had turned, because a house already begun gets finished. And so the pile of new homes nobody had bought kept growing. At its worst, in January 2009, it would have taken 12.2 months to sell them all at the pace they were selling: three years after the building had peaked. And then the builders, burned, held back for a decade. Starts did not reach one and a half million a year again until December 2019.

Who came out ahead? The builders that cut back hard in the bust, and could still pay their bills. D.R. Horton, a Texas homebuilder, sold 3.7 billion dollars of homes in its fiscal year 2009, and lost 0.55 billion. It kept going through the years when few houses were started. By fiscal 2024 it sold 36.8 billion dollars of homes in a year and made 4.8 billion of profit. Getting through the bust was the first step to winning the boom that followed.
Bullwhip: Cycles do not need a long wait to start. They can be manufactured out of almost nothing, inside a supply chain. Here is a shop. Its sales wobble a little from week to week, around a hundred. The shop orders from a wholesaler. It wants to keep two weeks of stock, and it guesses next week's sales from the last few weeks. When sales tick up, it orders the extra sales, plus extra to top up its stock for the higher sales it now expects. Its orders swing more than its sales. The wholesaler sees only those orders, and does the same thing to the factory. And the factory does it to its own suppliers. At every step up the chain the swings grow, until the company at the top is lurching between rush orders and none at all, while the shoppers at the bottom were buying about the same as always. In 1997 three researchers, Hau Lee, V. Padmanabhan and Seungjin Whang, named it the bullwhip effect: a small flick of the wrist, and a crack at the far end. They also described the cures, and the best-run supply chains use them. Share the shop's actual sales with every step up the chain, so each one sees real demand, not just the orders in front of it. Order smaller amounts, more often. And stop the price promotions that make shops buy in lumps.

You can see the whip in the national statistics. Take America's retail sales, month by month, and measure how much they typically change from one month to the next: about 1.6 percent. Now do the same for the new orders that American factories receive. They move by 2.6 percent. The factories feel swings 1.6 times as large as the shops, though in the end every order is for something a customer will buy.

The whip cracked across the car industry in 2021. When the pandemic began, American car plants shut: in April 2020 output was about a fifth of February's. Buyers came back, and by early 2021 output had recovered. Then it fell again, through the autumn, by about a sixth. Not for lack of buyers, but for lack of chips. Companies that buy chips told the Commerce Department that their median stock had fallen from 40 days' worth in 2019 to less than 5 in 2021. With few new cars to be had, the price of used cars rose by 53 percent between February 2020 and January 2022. A brief fall in demand at one end of a long chain had become a long shortage at the other.
Leverage: When the cycle turns, sales fall. Why do profits fall so much more? Take a business with a hundred dollars of sales. Half its costs move with sales: materials, energy, the people paid by the hour. Thirty dollars are fixed: the plant and its wear, which cost the same however much it makes. That leaves twenty dollars of profit. Now sales fall by a fifth. The costs that follow sales fall by a fifth too. The fixed costs do not move. Profit halves, from twenty to ten. That is operating leverage: the more of a business's costs are fixed, the harder a fall in sales hits its profit. Ships, chip plants and mines are almost all fixed cost. And there is a second lever. Suppose the business borrowed to build its plant, at the top of the cycle, and owes six dollars of interest a year. Interest is fixed too. Profit after interest falls from fourteen to four: by more than two thirds. The companies that borrowed most in the boom are the ones that fail in the bust.

Here is what that looks like in real accounts. In Micron's fiscal 2023, its sales fell by about half, from 30.8 billion dollars to 15.5 billion. Its operating profit of 9.7 billion became a loss of 5.7 billion, while its depreciation, the cost of the plants it had already built, went up. Maersk, the same year: sales down 37 percent, operating profit down 87 percent, and depreciation up. A business that is mostly plant cannot shrink its costs as fast as its customers shrink their orders. There is one comfort in a business made of plant. Depreciation is a cost in the accounts, but no cash leaves the bank for it: the cash went out years before, when the plant was built. So in fiscal 2023, while Micron lost 5.7 billion dollars on its operations, those operations still brought in 1.6 billion of cash, and it kept spending 7.7 billion on new plant through the trough. That is Part 3's cash statement at work: the companies that survive a bust are the ones whose cash keeps coming when their profits do not.
Oil: Oil runs on the same loop, with one more twist: the price is set for the whole world at once. For most of 2011 to 2014, a barrel of American crude sold for around a hundred dollars. The oil companies did what high prices tell them to do. Exxon Mobil, the largest American one, spent 34 billion dollars in 2012 on new wells, platforms and plants. Drillers opened up America's shale fields, and the country's output of crude rose from 5.5 million barrels a day in 2010 to 9.4 million in 2015. The new oil arrived. In June 2014 a barrel cost 106 dollars; by February 2016, 30. Exxon cut its spending to 16 billion, less than half. Then came the pandemic: in April 2020, with the world's roads emptied, a barrel averaged 17 dollars for the month, and Exxon's spending fell to 12 billion the year after. Spending stayed low, and when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the price shot back above a hundred dollars. The spending has been climbing ever since. Each turn of the wheel is set up by the one before.
Reading: Chapter thirteen. Reading where you are.

If you cannot stop the cycle, you can at least try to read it. A handful of gauges help. First, the order book: how much new capacity is already on its way, compared with what exists. In shipping it read 52 percent in 2009, with the boom's orders still arriving, and 19 percent in 2014. In early 2025 it read 15, and rising. Second, spending against wear: what a company spends on new plant, against its depreciation. Near one, it is just replacing what wears out. Micron's reading in fiscal 2026 was 3.2, its highest since at least 2010. Third, unsold stock. At the end of fiscal 2023, Micron held chips worth 6.5 months of its sales; at the end of fiscal 2026, under one month: 0.9. Shelves that empty are what a peak looks like. Fourth, for houses, the months it would take to sell every new home for sale: 12.2 at the worst, in January 2009; 8.4 in September 2026. None of these says when a cycle will turn. Together, they say how much is coming, and how little room there is if demand stops growing. For memory chips, the one to watch is the third: when Micron's stock of unsold chips climbs back from under one month of sales toward the two or three months it held in calmer years, buyers will have stopped scrambling, and prices will follow.
Ai: Chapter fourteen. A boom you can watch.

Everything in this part says you cannot know when a cycle will turn. But you can watch one being built. Here are four of the companies spending most on data centres for artificial intelligence: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta. In 2015, between them, they spent 23 billion dollars on buildings and equipment. By 2020, 93 billion. In 2025, 358 billion: more than fifteen times as much in ten years. Amazon's figure includes its warehouses. And Microsoft's next year, to June 2026, came in at 116 billion on its own.

Now read the gauges from chapter thirteen. Spending against wear: in 2025 the four spent 2.8 times their depreciation, up from 1.7 in 2023. They are not replacing plant; they are building a new layer of it. And they are paying for it with their own cash: about 64 cents of every dollar their businesses brought in went back into building, up from 41 two years earlier. Those readings look like the top of a capital cycle. They are also what the start of a long build-out looks like, when a new technology really does need new plant, as railways and electricity once did. The gauges cannot tell the two apart. What decides it is whether what customers spend on artificial intelligence grows as fast as the plant being built for it. And that, unlike the spending, is not yet in anyone's accounts. The memory chips of chapter seven are the same boom, seen from a supplier's side.
Called: Every part ends with a forecast. This one is a decision made at a peak. In March 2021, in the middle of a worldwide shortage of chips, Intel's new chief executive, Pat Gelsinger, announced a plan to build its way back to the front of the industry, starting with about twenty billion dollars for two new factories in Arizona. Intel's spending on plant rose from 14.3 billion dollars in 2020 to 25.8 billion in 2023. Its operating profit went the other way: from 19.5 billion in 2021 to a loss of 11.7 billion in 2024. The shortage passed, and the new factories were costs long before they were revenue. In 2025 Intel cut its spending to 14.6 billion. A plan drawn up at a peak, with the peak's numbers, met the trough.

And this series' own call, logged today. Before the end of 2028, Micron will report a quarter whose revenue is at least a quarter below the best quarter before it. So far that is 54.2 billion dollars, the quarter to September 2026. The case for: after every one of its four earlier peaks, Micron's quarterly revenue fell by a fifth or more within two years, and in three of the four by more than a quarter. And it is spending 3.2 times its depreciation. The case against: the demand from data centres for artificial intelligence may keep growing faster than the new factories can be built. We put it at fifty-five percent, and will score it from Micron's own reports in January 2029. The early signs will come before that, every quarter: Micron's stock of unsold chips, its forecast for the next quarter, and what the data-centre builders of chapter fourteen say they will spend. If those turn, the call is on its way to coming true. If they do not, this boom is the exception, and the rest of this series will have to explain why.
